name: Eiffel
title: Eiffel (ECMA-367 / ISO/IEC 25436:2006)

presenceList.meta: R2, Ec3, Ec4, D1, L1, S1

preamble.text: Analysis against the Eiffel language standard (ECMA-367, approved June 2005; ISO/IEC 25436:2006) and EiffelStudio 25.12 (January 2026). Eiffel, created by Bertrand Meyer, is the language that introduced Design by Contract.

type.text: **Design by Contract (DBC)**: `require` (preconditions), `ensure` (postconditions), and `invariant` (class invariants) make an element's *change conditions* explicit. This is the coupling-relevant feature: contracts name the requirements an element realizes, so a change in one element's requirements that forces another element's contract to change is visible at the boundary
**Void safety (attached types)**: `x: attached T` vs `x: detachable T` separates non-null from nullable at compile time (Eiffel 6+). Eliminates the null-checking coupling class at compile time
**Strong static typing**: No implicit coercion, no unchecked casts as escape hatches

**No argument overloading**: Each feature name within a class maps to exactly one feature — "one name, within one class, means one thing." This eliminates method-resolution ambiguity coupling and is what makes Eiffel's multiple inheritance safe

**Command-Query Separation**: Queries (which return information) must not modify the instance — a Meyer design rule that prevents side effects hidden in value retrieval from coupling unrelated elements
**Generics with constraints**: `LINKED_LIST [G -> COMPARABLE]` decouples containers from element types
**Multiple inheritance**: Supported with `rename`, `redefine`, and `select` — powerful feature reuse but creates hierarchy coupling and diamond complexity
**Inheritance still available**: Class hierarchies couple behavior to the inheritance tree

construction.text: **Creation procedures (`create`)**: Separate allocation from initialization; `create x.make(...)`
**Invariants validate object state**: `invariant` clauses check well-formedness after every feature call
**Creation procedures can have side effects**: Nothing enforces pure construction

**Once routines create global singleton state**: `once` routines run once (per thread by default, configurable per process or per object) and cache their result — a memoized shared-state coupling across the system

memory.text: **Automatic GC**: No manual deallocation, no use-after-free, no dangling pointers
**No pointers**: Memory safety by construction; expanded types give value semantics
**GC pauses**: Non-deterministic, couple timing-sensitive code to runtime
**Void references possible (legacy code)**: Without attached-type discipline, dereferencing a void reference raises a `Void_call` exception at runtime

error.text: **Rescue/retry**: Structured exception handling where `rescue` + `retry` separates error recovery from error detection — failure handling decoupled from the code that triggered it
**Contract-driven exceptions**: Exceptions arise from precondition/postcondition/invariant violations, making failure points explicit and first-class rather than accidental
**Exceptions not used for control flow**: Eiffel treats exceptions as contract failures, so error recovery is limited to what the contract model supports

**Contracts can be disabled at compile time**: EiffelStudio can compile an executable to include or exclude any set of contracts (workbench vs. deployment modes), coupling correctness to build configuration

concurrency.text: **SCOOP (Simple Concurrent Object-Oriented Programming)**: Separates concurrency from logic via processor- and handler-oriented design; decouples "what runs concurrently" from "how it synchronizes" (e.g. multiple threads without explicit mutex management). Available in EiffelStudio, though not yet part of the official language definition
**Agents**: Wrap operations into objects, closely connected with closures and lambda calculus — decoupling callbacks from the calling code
**SCOOP is complex and niche**: Correct concurrent design requires deep expertise; low adoption
**Shared mutable state possible**: No compiler-level race detection

platform.text: **Native compilation without a runtime**: EiffelStudio compiles to a native executable, so a deployed program does not depend on a vendor runtime
**Portable across the major desktop platforms**: EiffelStudio targets Windows, Linux, and macOS

**One vendor owns the ISO-conforming implementation**: EiffelStudio is the ISO-conforming implementation and is commercial software from Eiffel Software, so the platform's evolution depends on that single vendor

performance.text: **Compiled to native code**: EiffelStudio generates efficient native executables
**GC pauses**: Non-deterministic, though modern GCs keep them short
**Contract overhead**: Runtime checks add cost; disablement improves performance but removes guarantees
**Deterministic when contracts disabled**: Predictable execution in deployment mode

ecosystem.text: **Small ecosystem**: Far fewer libraries than the JVM or .NET, so a solution couples to the few that exist and to a niche community
**EiffelStudio is a complete IDE**: Integrated compiler, debugger, and contract-aware tooling
**Dated tooling**: Modern build systems and package managers are weak relative to mainstream
**Niche community**: Limited third-party support and resources

**Fragmented implementations**: EiffelStudio, "The Eiffel Compiler" (tecomp), Gobo Eiffel, SmartEiffel, and LibertyEiffel differ; the GNU implementations track an older language version and do not fully implement the ISO standard

evolution.text: **ISO/ECMA standard**: Eiffel is an ISO/IEC standard (ISO/IEC 25436:2006, ECMA-367), giving a stable language core
**Slow, conservative evolution**: The standard is stable but innovation is glacial
**Implementations diverge**: EiffelStudio and the GNU-based implementations have drifted on language features
**Niche survival concern**: Long-term support depends on a small commercial base

domain.text: **Excellent for high-integrity and contract-heavy domains**: DBC is ideal where correctness is paramount and reliability is the design goal
**Good for teaching design-by-contract**: The language enforces the discipline
**Poor for mainstream web/systems**: GC, niche ecosystem, dated tooling
**Little adoption in modern development**: Hard to hire for

learning.text: **DBC is a clear mental model**: Contracts make intent explicit
**Multiple inheritance + renaming complexity**: Advanced Eiffel is hard to master
**SCOOP adds a second learning curve**: The concurrency model is non-trivial
**Fewer modern resources**: Documentation is dated relative to mainstream languages

syntax.text: **Readable, English-like**: `if x then ... else ... end`, `require`/`ensure`/`invariant` read naturally
**Explicit contracts**: The syntax makes specification a visible part of every feature
**Verbose**: `end` clauses and full declarations add ceremony
**Non-standard keywords**: Keywords (e.g. `feature`, `deferred`, `attached`) are unfamiliar to most programmers

testing.text: **Contracts enable automated testing**: preconditions/postconditions/invariants act as built-in test assertions
**EiffelStudio debugger**: Contract-aware, can inspect invariant violations
**Exception handling tools**: rescue/retry makes error paths debuggable
**Few third-party test frameworks**: The ecosystem is thin

security.text: **Memory safe**: GC, no pointers, no use-after-free, no buffer overflows
**Void safety**: Prevents null-pointer vulnerabilities by default (with attached types)
**No argument overloading**: Unambiguous feature resolution reduces surprising dispatch
**Once-routine shared state**: Can create hidden shared-state vulnerabilities

tradeoffs: **Contract vs. Runtime Cost**: Contract checking adds overhead; disabling it (deployment mode) removes the enforcement
**Inheritance vs. Composition**: Eiffel encourages inheritance as its primary reuse mechanism; multiple inheritance couples but enables precise feature reuse via renaming
**SCOOP vs. Pragmatism**: The concurrency model is elegant and low-coupling but hard to adopt in practice
**Once Routines vs. Independent Units**: Memoization decouples repeated computation but couples the element to global shared state that other elements may depend on
**Contract Depth vs. Discipline**: DBC only helps if teams actually write contracts; without them Eiffel degenerates to a plain typed OOP language
verdict: Eiffel's Design by Contract is the strongest contract-based coupling tool any mainstream-adjacent OOP language offers: it states each routine's obligations and guarantees in the source, so a boundary change is detected at the contract level rather than hidden in implementation. Void safety removes a whole null-checking coupling class that Java and C# still carry. The no-argument-overloading rule and Command-Query Separation eliminate two specific coupling hazards (ambiguous dispatch, hidden side effects). Main strength: DBC + void safety expose and prevent coupling better than almost any OOP language. Main weakness: niche ecosystem, once routines create shared state, and contracts are only as good as the discipline that writes them.

energy.text: Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy; @pereira2021ranking]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

use:desktop.observation: Portable across the major desktop platforms
